title: Tolliver and the Mixed-Up Signs
markdown:
The Amberglow Mountains were usually very quiet and warm under the moon. Tolliver, a big ogre with shoulders as wide and soft as a favourite chair, walked slowly through the bluebell wood. His large feet wore soft green boots. They made hardly any sound on the damp earth. Beside him hopped Fiver, a little rabbit. Fiver’s fur was the soft colour of cream. His long ears twitched at every tiny sound, like a moth’s wing or a sleepy owl’s hoot. Tolliver hummed a low rumbling song, soft like pebbles in a gentle stream. It was a song for walking under the moon.

“Look, Fiver.” Tolliver pointed a big green finger at a signpost. Yesterday it said To the Whispering Falls. But tonight the moonbeams showed it pointing to a patch of plump mushrooms. It was like an invitation for a midnight snack. Fiver wiggled his nose. His whiskers quivered. “Hoppity hop,” he squeaked. It meant, that is not right, Tolliver. Not even a little bit. Tolliver’s brow made a thoughtful line. “Someone has moved our signposts.” It was a gentle wondering whisper. “This is very strange. Let’s look. Maybe we can find out who is playing this moonlight game.”

They followed a winding path. The bluebells below looked like soft glowing carpet in the moonlight. Deeper in the woods they saw another signpost. It usually pointed to Tolliver’s napping rock. But tonight it pointed firmly towards a grumpy badger’s home. Tolliver always stayed away from there. Badgers grumbled a lot and had sharp tempers. Tolliver let out a soft sigh, like a gentle breeze. “This is very strange.” Just then they heard a soft rustling. Peeking through the moonlit branches, they saw a kind figure gathering leaves. It was Elara, the wise witch. Her basket was full of moon-kissed leaves and dewy petals. “Good evening, Elara. Have you seen anyone moving the signposts? They are pointing in all sorts of wrong directions.” Elara smiled. Her eyes twinkled like stars. “Ah, Tolliver, my dear boy. I saw a little fellow bustling about. He was moving them, yes, but he looked so lost and hurried. Bless him.”

Tolliver’s kind heart wished for everything to be just right. He liked things to be in their proper places. “Oh dear. Could you tell us where he went, please?” Fiver hopped close to Tolliver’s leg. His soft nose nudged him, a silent sign of support. Elara nodded. “He was muttering about needing a shortcut, bless his forgetful heart. He is a gnome, Glimmer. He often forgets which way is which when he is in a hurry.” Tolliver’s smile returned, warm and wide. “A gnome. Of course. It is no trouble. Fiver and I can help him find his way.” He thanked Elara.

Tolliver and Fiver followed a trail of disturbed leaves. Their footsteps were soft on the moss. They soon found Glimmer. He looked very flustered. He stood by a signpost pointing straight up, as if asking the moon for directions. “Hello, Glimmer. We are here to help. Your shortcuts have made our path a little wobbly. The bluebells are quite confused.” Glimmer’s tiny eyes widened. He wrung his small hands. “Oh dear. I have done it again, haven’t I? I was only trying to get home quickly for some warm milk, but I got all turned around.” Tolliver and Fiver patiently helped Glimmer. They showed him the right way. Glimmer was so grateful. Soon the signposts stood tall and pointed the right way. Elara, who had quietly followed, clapped her hands softly. “Well done, my dears.”

As dawn began to paint the sky pink and gold, Tolliver and Fiver hopped home. The bluebell wood felt peaceful. The signposts stood like friendly guides. Tolliver sat in his favourite armchair. It felt even cozier after their little adventure. Fiver curled up on his lap, a warm bundle of happiness. The soft warm feeling of home and safety washed over them. Soon, with contented sighs, they both drifted off to sleep. The napping rock pointed to itself again. The mushrooms could wait until morning.
characters: Tolliver (young ogre who walks under the moon), Fiver (a cream-furred rabbit with twitching ears)
author: StoryGen Community
